This scenario makes the battery eligible to be charged anytime the EV is at home if the SOC is below the maximum level. Whether the charging happens and at what power level is managed by the battery and charger modeling. Additionally, not all EV owners are modeled as charging exclusively at home. The 2020 RECS included a question about what fraction of charging is done at home, with the options being 100%, 80% to 99%, 60% to 79%, etc., which was translated to a ResStock input file and sampled to assign the “Home Charging Fraction” input. This input scales the average energy consumption rate of the battery model, ensuring that the resulting charging energy reflects only the portion of charging that occurs at home. The charging power remains fixed regardless of the at-home charging fraction, and only the vehicle discharge power is affected. The underlying assumption in using this approach is that 2020 RECS respondents implement the fraction of their charging in terms of energy, as opposed to time. EV charging and discharging energy are modeled within OpenStudio-HPXML, which leverages a lithium-ion battery model in EnergyPlus®. The “Electric Vehicle Charger” input directly influences charging power draw, which is assigned a constant value dependent on the charger level. The L2 charger type in this measure has a power draw of 5.69 kilowatts, which reflects the average EV charging power output of a 240-volt outlet. The other ResStock inputs in Table 2 influence the average EV energy consumption rate as well as the duration of driving events, which will reflect in the duration and energy demand of charging events. The “Home Charging Fraction” input adjusts for the actual charging energy provided by the at-home charger, however, we do not directly alter the number charging events but instead scale the average EV energy consumption rate. The average EV energy consumption rate can be considered the average driving power output under design conditions. Calculating the average EV energy consumption rate by dividing the annual discharge energy (kilowatt-hours) by the number of hours driven per year. Although we do not include all time-dependent variables impacting discharge events, we do incorporate a model that adjusts the average EV energy consumption based on the dwelling unit site ambient temperature at each time step. Ambient temperature plays a large role in EV energy usage, attributed primarily to the climate control systems of the vehicle cabin and battery.
